questions.question: A number line is drawn from 0 to 1 and split into 8 equal parts. Maya puts her dot on the 3rd mark after 0, Leo puts his dot on the 6th mark after 0, and Priya puts her dot on the 5th mark after 0. Reading the number line from left to right, in which order do the dots come?
questions.explain: The parts are all eighths, so the mark numbers give the fractions 3/8, 6/8 and 5/8, and you just order the numerators: 3, 5, 6. The common trap is reading right to left and giving the biggest fraction first — on a number line, left to right always means least to greatest.

questions.question: On a class map, the seawall path is a number line from 0 to 1 that is split into 10 equal parts. A water fountain sits on the 9th mark after 0, a bench sits on the 2nd mark after 0, and a bike rack sits on the 5th mark after 0. Which list puts the three fractions in order from greatest to least?
questions.explain: All three marks are tenths, so compare the numerators: 9 > 5 > 2, giving 9/10, 5/10, 2/10. The usual slip is listing them least to greatest out of habit — check whether the question asks for greatest first or least first.

questions.question: Three number lines of exactly the same length are drawn, and each one runs from 0 to 1. Line A is split into 2 equal parts with a dot on the 1st mark after 0. Line B is split into 8 equal parts with a dot on the 5th mark after 0. Line C is split into 4 equal parts with a dot on the 3rd mark after 0. If the lines were stacked on top of each other, which list puts the dots in order from the one closest to 0 to the one closest to 1?
options: Line C (3/4), Line B (5/8), Line A (1/2)
Line A (1/2), Line C (3/4), Line B (5/8)
Line A (1/2), Line B (5/8), Line C (3/4)
Line B (5/8), Line A (1/2), Line C (3/4)
questions.explain: Rename every dot in eighths because the lines are the same length: 1/2 = 4/8, 5/8 stays 5/8, and 3/4 = 6/8, so the order is 4/8, 5/8, 6/8. The common trap is thinking the one that says 5/8 is the largest because 5 and 8 are the biggest-looking numbers — you must use a common denominator first.

questions.question: Two number lines of the same length both run from 0 to 1. Line P is split into 5 equal parts and has a star on the 2nd mark after 0. Line Q is split into 10 equal parts and has a triangle on the 3rd mark after 0 and a square on the 7th mark after 0. Which list puts the three shapes in order from least to greatest?
questions.explain: Change 2/5 into tenths by splitting each fifth in half: 2/5 = 4/10, so you are ordering 3/10, 4/10 and 7/10. The common mistake is deciding 3/10 is bigger than 2/5 just because 3 > 2 — the pieces are different sizes until you make the denominators match.

questions.question: Order the fractions 5/6, 2/3 and 3/4 from least to greatest.
questions.explain: Twelve works as a common denominator: 5/6 = 10/12, 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12, so the order is 8/12, 9/12, 10/12. A frequent error is comparing numerators alone (2, 3, 5) and landing on 2/3, 3/4, 5/6 by luck or on 2/3, 5/6, 3/4 by mistake — always rename first, then compare.

questions.question: Nadia, Owen and Priya each bought the same size juice box at the school fun fair for $2. Nadia has 2/5 of her juice left, Owen has 1/2 left, and Priya has 7/10 left. Which list puts the amounts left from least to greatest?
questions.explain: Rewrite everything in tenths: 2/5 = 4/10, 1/2 = 5/10, and 7/10 stays 7/10, so the order is 4/10, 5/10, 7/10. The usual trap is putting the one that says 1/2 first because its numerator 1 is smallest — the boxes are the same size, so compare the renamed fractions, not the bare numerators.

questions.question: Use the benchmarks 0, 1/2 and 1 to order these three fractions from least to greatest: 7/8, 1/10, 4/9.
questions.explain: Check each against the benchmarks: 1/10 is close to 0, 4/9 is just under 1/2 because half of 9 is 4.5, and 7/8 is close to 1, so the order is 1/10, 4/9, 7/8. The common trap is calling 4/9 the smallest because 4 and 9 look small — benchmarks compare each fraction to a half, not to the other fractions' digits.

questions.question: Talia needs to put 5/12, 1/3 and 3/4 of a cup of berries in order from least to greatest. Which is the best first step for her to take?
options: Compare just the numerators 5, 1 and 3, because a bigger numerator always means a bigger fraction.
Compare just the denominators 12, 3 and 4, because a bigger denominator always means a bigger fraction.
Add the numerators together and the denominators together to make one new fraction, then compare it to 1/2.
Rewrite each fraction with the denominator 12 to get 5/12, 4/12 and 9/12, then compare the numerators.
questions.explain: Since 3 and 4 both divide into 12, rename them all in twelfths: 1/3 = 4/12 and 3/4 = 9/12, giving 4/12, 5/12, 9/12. Numerators alone only work when the denominators already match, and adding numerators and denominators straight across is never a way to compare fractions.

questions.question: Sofia is sorting three ribbons for an art project. The first is 2/3 of a metre, the second is 5/8 of a metre, and the third is 3/4 of a metre. She says that the bigger the denominator, the smaller the fraction, so she lists them as 5/8, 3/4, 2/3 from shortest to longest. Which list is actually correct from shortest to longest?
questions.explain: Use 24 as the common denominator: 2/3 = 16/24, 5/8 = 15/24 and 3/4 = 18/24, so the order is 15/24, 16/24, 18/24. Sofia's rule about denominators only works when the numerators are the same — here it makes her swap 2/3 and 3/4.

questions.question: A Grade 4 class in Surrey is checking four recycling bins that are all the same size. The paper bin is 5/6 full, the plastic bin is 3/4 full, the can bin is 2/3 full, and the compost bin is 7/12 full. Which list puts the bins in order from fullest to emptiest?
questions.explain: Rename all four in twelfths: 5/6 = 10/12, 3/4 = 9/12, 2/3 = 8/12 and 7/12 stays 7/12, so fullest to emptiest is 10/12, 9/12, 8/12, 7/12. The common trap is putting the one that says 7/12 first because 7 and 12 are the biggest numbers written down — the bins are the same size, so only the renamed fractions decide the order.

questions.question: Four students each ran part of the same 1 km track loop at their Kelowna school. Ana ran 5/8 of the loop, Ben ran 1/2 of the loop, Cara ran 2/3 of the loop, and Dev ran 3/4 of the loop. Who ran the second-farthest?
options: Dev, who ran 3/4 of the loop
Ana, who ran 5/8 of the loop
Cara, who ran 2/3 of the loop
Ben, who ran 1/2 of the loop
questions.explain: Rename in twenty-fourths: 5/8 = 15/24, 1/2 = 12/24, 2/3 = 16/24 and 3/4 = 18/24, so the order from farthest is 18/24, 16/24, 15/24, 12/24 and second place is 2/3. Many students stop after finding the longest distance, or pick the one that says 5/8 because 15/24 and 16/24 look close — order the whole set, then count to the second one.

questions.question: Three classes each had a $200 bottle-drive goal. Division 4A has reached 5/6 of its goal, Division 4B has reached 7/8, and Division 4C has reached 9/10. Which list puts the classes in order from the least of the goal reached to the most?
questions.explain: Each class is exactly one piece short of its goal, and the missing pieces are 1/6, 1/8 and 1/10; since 1/6 is the biggest missing piece, 5/6 is the least, then 7/8, then 9/10. The common trap is the rule that a bigger denominator always makes a smaller fraction, which wrongly puts 9/10 first — that rule only applies when the numerators match.
